Formants: What Makes a Vowel

What makes one vowel sound different from another: F1 and F2, the third formant, the singer’s formant and formant tuning, heard on a synthesised voice.

Sing ee and then ah on the same note. The pitch stays the same, yet anyone can hear which vowel is which. Your vocal folds make the same buzz both times; what changes is the shape of the tube above them, and that tube boosts some frequencies and damps others. The boosted regions are the formants, numbered from the bottom: F1, F2, F3 and so on. Two of them, F1 and F2, are enough to tell most vowels apart, and they line up closely with the vowel chart singers already use. This lesson takes you through them with a synthesised voice. Click a section’s heading to fold it; the “On this page” bar at the right jumps to any section and opens it.

How to use the page. Each widget has a ▶ button that starts a sustained voice and ■ to stop it (only one plays at a time; start with your volume low). The pictures are spectra: frequency runs left to right up to 4 kHz, each vertical line is one harmonic of the voice, and the curve is the filter the vocal tract puts on top. The same synthesiser drives the vowel chart on the IPA chart, where you can drag through the vowel space.

1. Source and filter

The voice is two things in a row. The source is the vocal folds: they open and shut at the pitch you sing, so they make a buzz at that pitch plus every whole-number multiple of it (the harmonic series), each one a little quieter than the one below. The filter is the throat, mouth and lips: a tube about 17 cm long in an adult, and like any tube it resonates at certain frequencies. Where it resonates, the harmonics come through strongly; between resonances they are damped.

The pitch belongs to the source and the vowel belongs to the filter, which is why you can sing any vowel on any note. Play the buzz on its own, then put a vowel’s filter on it.

The buzz is rich but has no vowel. With the filter on, the harmonics near each peak of the curve stand out, and that pattern of peaks is what your ear reads as a vowel. Change the pitch: the harmonic lines get closer or further apart, but the curve, and the vowel, stays where it is.

2. F1: tongue height and jaw

The first formant, F1, is the lowest peak, between about 250 Hz and 850 Hz. It follows how open the vocal tract is: a close vowel like [i] or [u] has a low F1, an open vowel like [a] a high one. Dropping the jaw and lowering the tongue raises F1.

Slide F1 up with F2 high and you go from [i] through [e] and [ɛ] towards [a]. With F2 low you go from [u] through [o] towards [ɔ] and [ɑ]. On the vowel chart, F1 is the vertical axis: close at the top, open at the bottom.

3. F2: front and back

The second formant, F2, runs from about 700 Hz to 2400 Hz. It follows where the tongue is bunched: forward in the mouth gives a high F2 ([i], [e]), back gives a low F2 ([u], [o]). Rounding the lips lengthens the tube and pulls F2 (and F3) down, so a rounded front vowel like [y] sits between [i] and [u].

On the vowel chart, F2 is the horizontal axis, with high F2 (front) on the left. Try holding F1 low and sweeping F2: [i] to [y] to [ɨ] to [u] is the whole top row of the chart.

4. The F1–F2 plane is the vowel chart

Put F1 down the page and F2 across it, high on the left, and the vowels fall into a shape that is close to the IPA trapezoid. The phonetics chart started as a map of the tongue; formant measurements in the twentieth century showed that it is just as much a map of sound. Drag anywhere in the plane.

The trapezoid shape comes from acoustics: front vowels can spread across a wide range of F2, while back vowels are squeezed into a narrow one, so the chart is wider at the top than at the bottom. The values here are averages for an adult male voice; a higher, shorter vocal tract (women, children) moves everything up by roughly 15–20 %, but the shape stays the same, which is how we hear the same vowel from different speakers.

Vowel Example F1 (Hz) F2 (Hz)
[i] see, Italian vino 280 2250
[e] German See, Italian sera 400 2100
[ɛ] bed 580 1850
[a] French patte, Italian casa 820 1550
[ɑ] father 760 1080
[ɔ] RP thought 600 900
[o] German so, Italian dove 430 750
[u] food, Italian luna 300 750
[ə] about 500 1450

5. F3, r-colouring and lip rounding

The third formant, F3 (around 2200–3000 Hz), changes less from vowel to vowel, but it carries two things. Lip rounding lowers it along with F2. And an r-coloured vowel, like the General American nurse [ɝ] or butter [ɚ], has a strikingly low F3, down near 1600 Hz, sitting just above F2. Drag F3 down on [ə] and listen to it turn into an American er.

F4 and above vary even less and mostly reflect the size of the singer’s head and throat: they are part of what makes a voice sound like that person.

6. The singer’s formant

Trained classical singers, especially men, make a strong peak around 2.5–3.2 kHz by clustering F3, F4 and F5 together, mostly by lowering the larynx and narrowing the tube just above the vocal folds. This singer’s formant is the “ring” or squillo that lets an unamplified voice carry over an orchestra: the orchestra is loudest below 1 kHz, and the ear is most sensitive near 3 kHz. Turn it on and off on the same vowel.

The vowel does not change, because F1 and F2 do not move. What changes is the brightness and the carrying power. Pop and musical theatre singers use the same region with a more speech-like vowel; a microphone means they need less of it.

7. High notes: when the pitch outruns the formants

The harmonics sample the filter curve only at multiples of the pitch. At a speaking pitch they are close together and trace the curve well. A soprano at 880 Hz has harmonics only at 880, 1760, 2640 Hz and so on, so F1 for [i] (about 300 Hz) is below the lowest note she can produce. No harmonic falls near it, and the vowel can’t be heard as [i] any more.

Raise the pitch on [i] and listen to the vowels blur together above about 600 Hz. Then turn on Tune F1 to the pitch: this raises F1 to just above the fundamental, which is what sopranos do by opening the jaw on high notes. It is called formant tuning, and it is the acoustic reason for vowel modification: a high [i] is sung towards [ɪ] or [e], and a high [u] towards [ʊ] or [o], so that F1 stays with the fundamental and the note keeps its power. The cost is that the vowel is less clear, and on the very highest notes listeners cannot tell vowels apart at all.

For singers: if a high note feels thin or hard on a closed vowel, open the jaw and let the vowel drift towards its open neighbour ([i]→[ɪ]→[e], [u]→[ʊ]→[o]). In the words, keep the consonants clear; they carry more of the meaning than the vowels do up there.

Things to try

  • In section 4, find your own vowels: say a word, hold the vowel, and hunt for it in the plane. Vowels in your accent may sit between the symbols.
  • In section 1, play [a] and drag the pitch slowly: the vowel stays put while the harmonics slide under the curve.
  • On the IPA chart, switch on Hold and click from [i] to [y] to [u]: one formant moves at a time.
  • In section 7, find the pitch where [i] and [e] stop sounding different without formant tuning.

Works Cited

For students

“Formant.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formant.

Nave, Carl R. “The Singing Formant.” HyperPhysics, Georgia State U, hyperphysics.gsu.edu/hbase/Music/singfor.html.

Truax, Barry, editor. “Formant.” Handbook for Acoustic Ecology, Simon Fraser U, www.sfu.ca/sonic-studio-webdav/handbook/Formant.html.

Wolfe, Joe, Maëva Garnier, and John Smith. “Voice Acoustics: An Introduction.” Music Acoustics, U of New South Wales, newt.phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/voice.html. Formants, the F1–F2 vowel map, the singer’s formant (2–4 kHz, F3–F5 clustered by lowering the larynx).

For teachers

Joliveau, Elodie, John Smith, and Joe Wolfe. “The Tuning of Vocal Tract Resonances by Sopranos.” Nature, vol. 427, 2004, p. 116. Summary at newt.phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/soprane.html. UNSW summary page read.

McCoy, Scott. Your Voice: An Inside View. Inside View Press, 2004. Later editions 2012 and 2019.

Sundberg, Johan. “The Acoustics of the Singing Voice.” Scientific American, vol. 236, no. 3, 1977, pp. 82–91. acousticslab.org/RECA220/PMFiles/PMDownloads/Sundberg1977_SingingVoice.pdf. Citation confirmed from JSTOR listing and citing pages; the singer’s formant at about 2–3 kHz.
